claims.claim: Eustathius of Antioch was the archbishop (patriarch) of Antioch from about 324 to 330 and was a native of Side in Pamphylia, dying in exile around 337.

The work traditionally called the Commentary on the Hexameron bears the name of Eustathius of Antioch but modern scholarship identifies its author as “Pseudo‑Eustathius” because the text contains material that could not have been written by the historical Eustathius, who was deposed in 330.
The commentary was composed in Greek sometime between the late fourth and early fifth centuries, roughly between 375 and 500 AD.
The author drew extensively on the Homilies on the Hexameron of Basil the Great (circa 370), as well as on Josephus and Achilles Tatius, showing a date later than Eustathius’s lifetime.
A modern critical edition was published by Friedrich Zoepfl in 1927.
The commentary is valuable because it preserves excerpts from the lost writings of Alexander Polyhistor and provides an early witness to the Christian bestiary known as the Physiologus.
